props.title: Blacula

sections.content: **Blacula** (1972) revolutionized Black horror cinema by brilliantly recasting vampire mythology through a racial lens. William Marshall's commanding performance as African Prince Mamuwalde, cursed by Dracula himself, brought gravitas to what could have been mere exploitation. The film cleverly uses vampire tropes to explore colonialism and racial identity, while its 1970s Los Angeles setting allows for pointed commentary on contemporary Black urban life. It spawned a wave of Black-centered horror including **Dr. Black, Mr. Hyde** (1976) and Ganja & Hess (1973), proving audiences were hungry for horror that spoke to African American experiences.

sections.content: The success of **Blacula** (1972) opened doors for Black filmmakers in horror. While mainstream critics initially dismissed it as exploitation, its sophisticated handling of racial themes and Marshall's dignified portrayal elevated it above standard drive-in fare. **Sugar Hill** (1974) followed with its voodoo-zombie revenge tale, while **Abby** (1974) reworked The Exorcist through a Black lens. These films created space for later works like **Tales from the Hood** (1995) and **Candyman** (1992) to explore racial horror in increasingly overt ways. SUBHEAD: Legacy and Influence

The film's impact extends well beyond the 1970s. Jordan Peele has cited **Blacula** (1972) as an influence on his approach to racial horror in **Get Out** (2017) and **Us** (2019). The character of Mamuwalde helped establish a template for Black vampires that influenced everything from Eddie Murphy's **Vampire in Brooklyn** (1995) to Wesley Snipes in **Blade** (1998). Modern films like **The Girl with All the Gifts** (2016) and **His House** (2020) continue Blacula's tradition of using horror to explore racial and colonial themes.
